Female Western dwarf galaxias reach an ultimate total length of 6.0 centimeters [Li = 6.0 centimeters], a modest size that is typical of species inhabiting seasonal freshwater systems in southwestern Australia. This maximum recorded length is achieved only under optimal conditions, and most individuals in the wild approach this value asymptotically over their lifetime. The total length at which females first attain puberty has been documented at 4.7 centimeters [Lp = 4.7 centimeters], representing approximately 78 percent of the ultimate length, a threshold that indicates a relatively late onset of reproductive capability compared with other small-bodied freshwater teleosts. Field surveys have confirmed that individuals below this size rarely exhibit macroscopic gonadal development, suggesting that energy allocation prior to this somatic milestone is directed primarily towards structural growth rather than gametogenesis. The progression from the size at puberty to the ultimate size appears to be a gradual process, with females continuing to grow incrementally after becoming reproductively active. This growth pattern is consistent with an iteroparous life history in which adults spread reproductive effort across multiple seasons, albeit constrained by the ephemeral nature of their habitat.

The reproductive strategy of Galaxiella munda is characterized by a moderately high output, with females producing approximately 65 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 65 eggs per clutch] during each spawning event. Field observations indicate that individual females typically deposit three clutches per year [F_R_i = three clutches per year] when maintained under the favorable thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a temperature that corresponds to the peak of the austral spring breeding period. Each clutch is deposited upon submerged vegetation, and the adhesive eggs develop rapidly under these conditions. The combination of a moderate clutch size and multiple spawning events per year yields a substantial annual fecundity, which helps offset the high rates of early-life mortality typical of pelagic larvae in unpredictable stream environments. The timing of these clutches appears tightly linked to photoperiod and rainfall cues, ensuring that larval emergence coincides with peak zooplankton abundance.

Neonates emerge from the adhesive eggs at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams]. This minute mass reflects the small diameter of the fertilized ova, which range from 1.1 to 1.4 millimeters in diameter, and places the species among the smallest-born freshwater fishes in the region. The lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva depends entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-eclosion, a critical period when the transparent, free-swimming larva remains vulnerable to predation. The rapid absorption of the yolk sac and the subsequent onset of exogenous feeding marks a pivotal transition in the early life history. Larvae begin feeding on rotifers and small copepod nauplii shortly after mouth opening, and growth during this pelagic larval phase is highly sensitive to water temperature and food availability. Survival through the yolk-sac stage is a major bottleneck in recruitment.

Adult females ultimately attain a maximum wet weight of 1.3 grams [Wwi = 1.3 grams] under favorable conditions, a value that is consistent with the allometric scaling relationship derived from the ultimate total length. This modest adult body mass is characteristic of the Galaxiellidae family, which occupy a low-trophic-level niche as microphagous planktivores and benthic invertebrate feeders. The energetic cost of achieving this body mass is relatively low, but the species compensates by investing heavily in reproductive tissue during the breeding season. Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that the wet weight at ultimate size is comparable to that of Galaxiella nigrostriata, though the latter attains a slightly shorter maximum length. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power function typical of fusiform teleosts, with condition factors varying seasonally in response to food availability and reproductive status. Field-collected specimens in peak spawning condition often exhibit particularly high mass for their length.

The maximum lifespan of Galaxiella munda in its natural habitat has been estimated at approximately 548 days [am = approximately 548 days] at an average water temperature of approximately 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a relatively short duration that underscores the species' adaptation to temporary water bodies. This constrained longevity, equivalent to roughly one and a half years, reflects the high metabolic costs associated with an active foraging lifestyle and the energetic demands of multiple reproductive bouts within a single season. Senescence becomes apparent in older individuals through a decline in body condition and reduced fecundity during the second breeding season. The annual mortality rate is consequently high, with very few individuals surviving to reproduce in a second year. This life history strategy, characterized by early maturation at a length of 4.7 centimeters [Lp = 4.7 centimeters] and a single reproductive window, aligns with that of an opportunistic strategist capable of rapidly colonizing newly inundated habitats following seasonal rains.
